title: POC weekly latency tuning - Rivermark
summary: Weekly POC sync to review latency benchmarking and tuning work. Focus on TTFT (time-to-first-token) wins from streaming, sequence-length handling, and kernel selection. SE presented kernel comparison numbers; customer raised concerns about cold-starts, VPC egress costs, and sequence length distribution in production. Agreed on additional bench runs and next checkpoint. Action items assigned.
next_steps: Redwood to run 2 more kernel comparison runs (FP16 vs 4-bit quant) at 2k seq and 512 seq and share results by 2028-09-13
Rivermark to provide 1 week of production seq-length histogram and request traces by 2028-09-11
Schedule deep-dive with infra team to validate VPC egress and routing by 2028-09-15
Redwood to share streaming/TTFT presentation and updated runbook (links) by EOD 2028-09-07
Set up a benchmark session with Aaron, Lena, and Diego for 2028-09-14
action_items: Diego Ramos: run kernel comparison FP16 vs 4-bit quant, sequences 512 & 2048; deliver results 2028-09-13
Maya Chen: send updated pricing for dedicated pool + burst nodes and sample SLA language by 2028-09-08

transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2028-09-06 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Aaron Patel (Rivermark CTO), Lena Cho (Lead ML Eng), Samir Khan (Infra), Priya Nair (PM)

Summary (auto): Weekly POC - focus on latency tuning, TTFT, streaming buffers, kernel selection.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick roll call?
[00:07] Aaron Patel: Aaron here.
[00:09] Lena Cho: Lena on call.
[00:11] Samir Khan: Samir.
[00:13] Priya Nair: Priya.
[00:15] Diego Ramos: Diego from Redwood.
[00:17] Maya Chen: Great. We blocked 45 minutes. Diego's going to walk through the kernel comparison results and then we'll triage where to run next.
[00:27] Diego Ramos: Cool, thanks. Quick note up front: transcription's a bit rough so if I say "KV cache" and it shows "kay vee" forgive me. Ok slide one - TTFT baseline. We re-ran the benchmark against your workload sample using the 1.5B open variant you gave us. Default streaming off, batch size 1, cold start. Median TTFT was ~220ms, p95 around 420ms. When we enabled streaming and reduced initial token prefetch to 1 token the TTFT dropped to ~95ms median. So streaming gives a ~2.3x improvement for first token.
[01:12] Lena Cho: Wait, is that with FP16 kernels or the quantized runtime?
[01:16] Diego Ramos: That baseline was FP16. The quantized run (4-bit) had slightly worse cold-start TTFT due to additional dequant steps on the first token, so cold TTFT was about 140ms median but steady-state token latency after a few tokens was slightly better.
[01:30] Aaron Patel: Hmm, cold-start is our biggest pain; our traffic is spiky at EOD. We care about first token for interactive flows.
[01:38] Maya Chen: Right, that's where warm pools and pre-warming come in — plus streaming. We showed pre-warm options in last week's deck, but Diego, can you remind on warm pool sizing?
[01:47] Diego Ramos: Sure. For your 99th percentile concurrency profile (estimated 35 concurrent), a small warm pool of 8-12 GPUs keeps TTFT within target for most spikes. There's tradeoff: cost vs cold-start pain. Also kernel choice matters: some kernels spend time on preloading weight pages which hurts cold TTFT.
[02:10] Samir Khan: Are those preloads over the network if we do Private VPC? Concerned about egress and firewall.
[02:18] Diego Ramos: For Private deployments, weights are local on the node, so preloads are disk->GPU. Egress only matters for control-plane operations, not token generation. But if you use external model registry we can cache locally to avoid egress.
[02:33] Lena Cho: Good to know. Could you run the kernel comparison with our exact AMI? We saw mismatches last run.
[02:40] Diego Ramos: We can — Maya, do we have their AMI/instance spec?
[02:43] Maya Chen: Samir shared the infra notes last week; Diego's got limited access via the test account.
[02:49] Samir Khan: Correct, test account has the same AMI and the network rules. I can open a secondary key for your SE if needed.
[02:56] Diego Ramos: Perfect. For the kernel numbers: we saw FP16 kernels had best cold TTFT, quant (4-bit) improved steady-state token latency by ~8-12%, but increased cold TTFT due to dequant overhead. Certain attention kernels (fused attention) help long sequences; others excel for short sequences.
[03:18] Priya Nair: On sequence lengths — our production 95th pct is about 1200 tokens, median ~220. Does that change recommended kernels?
[03:27] Diego Ramos: Yes. For median/short we recommend kernel set A (low-latency short-seq optimized). For 1k+ sequences kernel set B (fused attention + chunked KV) gives better throughput and memory behavior, but has slightly higher per-token latency on short sequences.
[03:45] Lena Cho: Can you quantify? like how much higher p50 token latency?
[03:49] Diego Ramos: On our tests kernel B p50 token latency was ~5-8% higher on 128-token slices compared to kernel A, but p95 and throughput for long sequences improved by ~20-30%.
[04:05] Aaron Patel: That sounds acceptable if we can keep TTFT low for our interactive flows. Any tuning knobs?
[04:11] Diego Ramos: Streaming + prefix caching helps. Also we can do an adaptive routing policy — short interactive requests hit a short-seq-optimized variant (lower memory, faster kernels), while long batchy requests route to long-seq-optimized nodes. That's something we can configure in the routing policy.
[04:26] Maya Chen: Aaron, you mentioned cost constraints earlier — do you have a hard cap on monthly commit for Dedicated?
[04:33] Aaron Patel: We have a committed budget of roughly $40k/mo for the pilot; we want to evaluate whether Dedicated makes sense vs Hosted.
[04:40] Maya Chen: Great, we'll model cost for a mixed routing setup and share numbers.
[04:44] Lena Cho: Back to kernels — are there kernel-level patches or updated CUDA kernels that could change the dequant penalty?
[04:51] Diego Ramos: There are ongoing improvements in our runtime: dequant path optimizations and fused dequant+matmul kernels. We have an internal branch that reduces dequant overhead on first token by ~30% but it's not GA. We can trial it in the POC if you allow a lab branch — but that has the usual caveats.
[05:10] Aaron Patel: Will that require additional validation for compliance? Our security team is strict.
[05:15] Maya Chen: We can run it in Redwood Dedicated test nodes with audit logging and limited access. Also we'll share the code diff and test logs. If needed, we can route just your non-sensitive workloads through it for benchmarking.
[05:27] Samir Khan: We need to see audit trail and SSO controls — anything touched by that branch must be logged.
[05:32] Diego Ramos: Understood, we'll enable verbose logging for that run and provide the artifacts.
[05:36] Priya Nair: A few quick questions from product side — if we do adaptive routing, how will we A/B test quality? We can't degrade responses for LLM quality.
[05:45] Diego Ramos: Good point. We can do canary rollout with automatic fallback: compare outputs on a sample of requests and run evals; if quality regression is detected beyond threshold, auto-fallback to the safer model variant. Redwood Optimize can run those evals and trigger alerts.
[06:00] Lena Cho: And do you have an ETA for the streaming runbook update?
[06:03] Maya Chen: We'll aim to get the doc out by EOD tomorrow and share a link in the repo.
[06:08] Diego Ramos: Ok jumping to the kernel comparison table I shared in the drive link — quick highlights: FP16 best cold TTFT, 4-bit best steady-state throughput. Fused attention kernel B better for >1k sequences.
[06:24] [screen share noise, inaudible 6 sec]
[06:31] Maya Chen: Sorry — screen share glitch. Diego keep going.
[06:35] Diego Ramos: No problem. We also experimented with different initial token chunk sizes for streaming; starting with 1 token gives best TTFT but slightly degrades early-context quality for some few-shot prompts because the model gets less immediate context. Starting with 4 tokens is a middle ground.
[06:55] Aaron Patel: Hmm, we have templated prompts that rely on a 4-turn context; risking quality drop is risky.
[07:02] Diego Ramos: Understood — we can test 1 vs 4 token prefetch on a representative prompt set to quantify output diffs.
[07:10] Priya Nair: Please include that in the benchmark matrix.
[07:13] Diego Ramos: Will do. Next up: warm pool sizing and cost modeling — we estimated warm pool cost for Dedicated and for hosted with pre-warmed tokenless containers. For your workload the sweet spot was a warm pool of 10 units in Dedicated which hit TTFT SLAs and stayed under the $40k/mo pilot commit if you allow some burst credits.
[07:37] Aaron Patel: Can you share the math? We want the per-req cost and also the incremental cost for raising concurrency 2x.
[07:45] Maya Chen: We'll attach the calculation sheet. Diego, note to send per-token cost and amortized warm pool cost.
[07:50] Diego Ramos: Noted.
[07:52] [08:00] Random crosstalk
[08:05] Lena Cho: technical note — our logs show a bimodal seq-length distribution; we can send a histogram.
[08:12] Diego Ramos: That will help with routing policy; we'll tune thresholds.
[08:16] Aaron Patel: Another ops question — cold-start isolation. If one request triggers a heavy long-seq run, does it block the warm pool and impact short interactive ones?
[08:27] Diego Ramos: By default no — we can isolate long-seq workloads to separate node pools or set request concurrency caps per node. Also the autoscaler can preferentially scale long-seq workers.
[08:37] Samir Khan: For Private on-prem, does Redwood require any egress to the control plane for metrics or do we have offline log push?
[08:45] Maya Chen: Metrics can be pushed to your internal observability or to Redwood; for air-gapped we support local metrics collection and periodic manual export. We'll document both.
[08:56] Priya Nair: Good. Any blockers from security on using the runtime branch?
[09:01] Diego Ramos: Only the usual for non-GA code — we need to run the branch under restricted access and provide logs.
[09:06] Aaron Patel: Okay let's agree on the concrete bench runs.
[09:09] Maya Chen: Diego can you summarize the bench matrix?
[09:12] Diego Ramos: Sure — matrix: (1) FP16 baseline cold+warm at seq 512 & 2048; (2) 4-bit quant cold+warm at seq 512 & 2048; (3) Branch kernel with dequant optimization at seq 512 cold; (4) Streaming prefetch 1 vs 4 tokens across those runs; (5) Warm pool sizes 6/10/14 for concurrency 35/70. We'll produce TTFT median/p95, token latency p50/p95, and throughput and memory footprint.
[09:44] Lena Cho: Sounds good. Can you include output quality diffs for streaming prefetch variants?
[09:49] Diego Ramos: Yes, we'll include automatic eval scores on your prompt set.
[09:53] Aaron Patel: Who's the owner for each run?
[09:55] Diego Ramos: Diego will run 1-3, Maya will coordinate, Samir to validate infra, Lena to validate quality results.
[10:03] Maya Chen: And we'll sync next week same time. If we have big changes we'll call sooner.
[10:08] Priya Nair: Quick note — include cost delta for enabling branch versus not.
[10:12] Diego Ramos: Will do.
[10:14] Maya Chen: Any other questions?
[10:16] Aaron Patel: None from me.
[10:18] Lena Cho: No.
[10:20] Samir Khan: All good.
[10:22] Maya Chen: Ok recap of next steps — Diego runs kernel benches, Lena provides histograms, Maya sends pricing and runbook, Samir opens key for SE if needed. We'll share links to results folder and schedule next sync. Thanks everyone.
[10:36] [meeting end]

References / artifacts mentioned: slides (link_shared_in_chat), kernel-comparison-sheet (drive link), streaming-runbook (repo link), pricing-sheet (link).

Notes on transcript quality: some words and proper nouns mis-transcribed (e.g., "KV cache" as "kay vee", some timestamps approximate).
